svg.title: Driver-negative analysis — 11 drivers
svg.text: 7,809 patients sequenced · drivers: EGFR, KRAS, ALK, ROS1, BRAF, MET, RET, ERBB2, NTRK1, NTRK2, NTRK3
Of the 7,809 patients of “NSCLC” sequenced for mutations, 4,911 (62.9%) carry an OncoKB driver (v7.5) — a called mutation, a high-level copy-number call or a
structural variant the store calls oncogenic or likely oncogenic — in EGFR, KRAS, ALK, ROS1, BRAF, MET, RET, ERBB2, NTRK1, NTRK2, NTRK3; 2,898 (37.1%) carry none
and were sequenced on a panel covering every one of those genes (or whole-exome): the driver-negative group. 0 (0.0%) carry none but were not profiled for every listed
gene, so are neither — kept out of both sides, never counted as driver-negative. Coverage is read from the mutation panels; a fusion driver is called only where the study
reports structural variants. Then every other gene's mutation frequency is compared between driver-negative and driver-positive patients, in PATIENTS over the patients
profiled for that gene (a panel that lists it, or whole-exome; an off-panel call counts as measured), two-sided Fisher's exact test, Benjamini–Hochberg q over the 487
genes tested; 7 altered genes were not tested (fewer than 5 altered patients, or not profiled in a group). The log ratio is log2 of the driver-negative share over the
driver-positive one. Driver-positive tumours are often mutually exclusive with other drivers by biology, so a gene enriched in the driver-negative group is a candidate
alternative driver, not a proven one; smoking history and tumour mutation burden also differ between the groups and are not adjusted for.
